title: Senior Home-Renovation Programs
summary: CREDITS → GRANTS → GATEWAY → APPLY IN ORDER
subtitle: There are three kinds of help for a renovation. Almost everyone only ever finds one.

blocks.text: You would never leave the house in a Canadian February wearing just a sweater. A senior renovation works the same way. One program is never the whole outfit, no matter how good that one program is.
Most people find one program, apply, and stop. That is usually where the money gets left behind.

There are three kinds of help: money back at tax time, grants and loans from your province or city, and a certificate that quietly unlocks more of both. This module walks through all three in the order that works, then shows you how to sort a real invoice so you claim every eligible dollar and nothing that will bounce back.
Using all three layers of help can cover much more of a safer home than any single program.
blocks.detail: A tax credit, a local grant and one certificate each pay at a different time and in a different way.
blocks.extra: Section 02 starts with money back at tax time.

sections.title: Layer One: Money Back at Tax Time

blocks.text: Two federal tax credits help pay for a renovation. People mix them up constantly, so here they are side by side.

items.title: Home Accessibility (HATC)
list: Permanent safety changes: a walk-in shower, a ramp, grab bars, a stair lift, wider doorways
For anyone 65 or older, or approved for the Disability Tax Credit
A family member who pays for the work can claim it instead
Non-refundable: it only lowers tax you already owe

items.title: Multigenerational (MHRTC)
list: Building a small apartment with its own door, kitchen, bathroom and bedroom
For a senior, or an adult approved for the Disability Tax Credit, to live with family
A nicely finished spare room does not count. It needs its own door
Refundable: it is paid even if you owe no tax

blocks.text: What the two credits are worth in 2026

items.title: HATC cost limit
items.text: $20,000 — of eligible costs a year, for each person the work is for.

items.title: HATC rate
items.text: 14% — the lowest federal tax rate in 2026, down from 15%. That makes the most it can save $2,800.

items.title: MHRTC
items.text: Up to $7,500 — 15% of up to $50,000 in eligible costs for one new suite.

blocks.text: Both credits show up the spring after the work is done, not when you pay the contractor. That gap between paying and getting paid back is where most of the trouble starts. You can claim both on the same project, but not for the same dollar.

items.title: “These are grants, they will pay for my renovation.”
items.text: Neither one pays a contractor. Both are tax credits you claim after the fact, and the amount depends on the tax rate, which changed in 2025 and 2026. Budget the full cost up front, and treat the credit like a rebate that arrives next spring.

blocks.text: Refundable and non-refundable are not fine print. They decide whether a senior gets money or gets nothing. A non-refundable credit can only lower tax you already owe. Many people living on Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement owe little or no tax, so the Home Accessibility Credit may be worth far less than it sounds. A refundable credit, like the Multigenerational credit, pays out either way. That is why the family member paying the bill often claims the non-refundable credit. Decide this before the invoice is written, not after.

items.title: Refundable or not decides whether you get money or nothing.
items.text: Refundable or not decides whether you get money or nothing.

blocks.text: CRA: Multigenerational Home Renovation Tax Credit

sections.title: Sort the Invoice Before You Claim It

blocks.text: A renovation invoice mixes costs that count with costs that do not. The Home Accessibility Credit covers permanent changes that help someone get around safely. It does not cover routine repairs, decoration or appliances, even when they happen in the same room on the same day.
Here is an example bathroom job, sorted line by line.
$13,100 of the $18,600 invoice counts. At 14%, that is a $1,834 credit.
blocks.extra: It is only worth $1,834 to someone who owes at least that much federal tax. That is the question to settle before deciding whose name goes on the claim.

items.title: Whole invoice
items.text: Does the contractor list each part of the job on its own line?

items.title: Walk-in shower and safety valve
items.text: Does it replace a tub that was a fall risk?

items.title: Wider bathroom door
items.text: Is the new width for a walker or wheelchair?

items.title: Grab bars and wall backing
items.text: Are they fixed to the wall, not suction cups?

items.title: Decorative tile and mirror
items.text: Would you have bought this even without the safety change?

items.title: Leaking pipe found during the job
items.text: Is this a routine repair rather than an accessibility change?

blocks.text: Ask the contractor for an invoice with every part of the job on its own line, the company’s GST/HST number and the home’s address. One total on one line forces you to guess, and a guess is hard to defend if the CRA asks.

items.title: “If the job was for accessibility, the whole bill counts.”
items.text: Only the parts that make the home safer or easier to get around count. Sorting the invoice yourself keeps a claim from being cut back later.

sections.title: Layer Two: Where the Real Grants Live

blocks.text: This is the layer most people never find, because it has no single name and no single website. These programs pay before the work starts, usually as a grant or a loan you never have to repay. Most of them check your income first. Some are run by the province. Many are run by your city or region for the province, which is why the same program can look different one town over.

items.title: British Columbia
items.text: A rebate for accessibility work, plus a renovation tax credit for seniors.

items.title: Alberta
items.text: The Seniors Home Adaptation and Repair Program. Read carefully: it is a loan against your home, not a grant.

items.title: Saskatchewan
items.text: A home renovation tax credit open to homeowners generally, not only seniors.

items.title: Ontario
items.text: Ontario Renovates, through your city or region: part grant, part loan. First-come, until the money runs out.

items.title: Quebec
items.text: Programme d’adaptation de domicile and RénoRégion, applied for through your municipality.

items.title: Atlantic Canada
items.text: New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, PEI and Newfoundland and Labrador each run their own seniors’ repair programs.

items.title: The Territories
items.text: Yukon and the Northwest Territories run seasonal programs. Miss the window, and you wait a year.

blocks.text: Two habits beat memorizing this list: search “home adaptation program” with your city’s name, and call 211. They keep the real, current local list.

items.title: “Grants are only for people with almost no income.”
items.text: Grant programs almost always check income, but the limit is often higher than people expect, well above what many seniors on a fixed income get. The tax credits do not check income at all. Assuming you make too much is how people skip both.

sections.title: Layer Three: One Form That Unlocks the Rest

blocks.text: The Disability Tax Credit (DTC) is not a renovation program on its own. It is a certificate. Your doctor or another approved health worker fills in a form that confirms a serious, long-term health condition. A surprising amount of the money in this course sits underneath it.

DTC approval opens the Home Accessibility Credit at any age, not just 65. It can make someone a qualifying person for the Multigenerational credit. It helps with, or is required for, several provincial grants. It can even be applied to past tax years, sometimes producing a refund large enough to help pay for the renovation outright.

It is also turned down the first time fairly often, then approved later once the health worker adds more detail. If anyone in the home has a long-term problem with moving, seeing, hearing or memory and has never applied, that is the best use of an hour in this whole course.
Does this apply to me?

items.title: Who
items.text: Someone in the home is 65 or older, or has a long-term health condition.

items.title: What
items.text: The work is permanent and about safety or getting around, not decoration.

items.title: Where
items.text: The home is the main residence of the person the work is for.

items.title: When
items.text: The work has not started yet, or every receipt has been kept.

items.title: Local
items.text: You have checked what your province and city offer, not just the federal credits.

items.title: Whose name
items.text: You know who in the family will pay, and who will claim the credit.

sections.title: Do These in Order, or the Money Disappears

blocks.text: Most of this money is lost by doing things in the wrong order. Grant programs usually will not pay for work that already started. Tax credits do not care about timing, but they care a great deal about receipts.

items.title: Apply for the DTC first, if it might fit
items.text: It can take months to hear back, and it changes what else you can get.

items.title: Find the rule about starting work
items.text: Read it before you accept a quote. If it says wait for written approval, that sentence matters more than any quote.

items.title: Get an assessment, if one is asked for
items.text: Some programs want an occupational therapist to sign off. It helps a tax claim too, even where it is not required.

items.title: Get written approval, then start
items.text: A phone call does not count. Neither does a friendly email from someone who is “pretty sure” it will go through.

items.title: Keep every receipt
items.text: It needs the company’s GST/HST number, the address, what was done, and proof you paid. A total on a business card is not a receipt.

items.title: Claim it at tax time
items.text: Tell whoever does your taxes that the work happened. They cannot claim what they do not know about.

items.title: “The contractor said he would handle the paperwork.”
items.text: Some contractors handle it well. But you sign the tax return, and you are the one a program holds to the start-work rule. Ask to see the written approval yourself before anyone touches a wall.

blocks.text: Every program in this course pays you back later, but the contractor wants to be paid now. That gap tempts people toward the fastest loan in the room, and the fastest loan in the room is almost always the worst one. Contractor financing, rent-to-own equipment and high-rate second mortgages are marketed hardest to the households these programs are meant to help. Cheaper options usually exist: a line of credit from your own bank, a written family loan, splitting the work across two tax years, or waiting for the next grant window.

Worth checking too: if a Veteran lives in the home, the Veteran Benefits lesson covers the Veterans Independence Program, which can also help with home support and changes, on entirely separate money from anything in this course.

sections.title: Two Sisters, One Bathroom, and a Rule in Paragraph Nine

blocks.text: Two sisters, one bathroom
paragraphs: Bernice is eighty-two and has lived in the same house in Moncton since 1974. Her daughters, Colette and Anne-Marie, agree the bathtub has to go before Bernice slips getting out of it. Colette gets three quotes. Anne-Marie, who reads things, gets the application forms.
Then the contractor calls. He has a cancellation and can start Monday. Colette is ready to say yes. Their mother’s safety feels more urgent than any form.

That one sentence has cost Canadian families more grant money than any other. Anne-Marie goes back to the guidelines. In paragraph nine, she finds the rule: work started before written approval will not count.

The sisters have to choose. Start Monday and lose the grant, or wait six weeks for approval. They pick the wait. Anne-Marie puts a non-slip mat and a grab bar in the old tub for now. The contractor is slightly annoyed.

They also get the math right. Bernice lives on Old Age Security, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and a small pension, so she pays almost no tax. A non-refundable credit in her name would be close to worthless. Colette pays for the work and claims the Home Accessibility Credit on her own return. Anne-Marie applies for the provincial grant in Bernice’s name, where the income test works in their favour.
The walk-in shower goes in that March. Between the grant and the credit, the family pays about half of the first quote.
Nothing clever happened. Two people read the rules, split the paperwork and decided who was paying before anyone bought tile.

items.title: MONDAY OFFER
items.text: Contractor can start early

items.title: PARAGRAPH NINE
items.text: No work before approval

items.title: SIX WEEKS LATER
items.text: Written approval arrives

blocks.text: Bernice’s family paid about half of the first quote by waiting for approval and choosing who claimed which credit.
blocks.detail: Reading the start-work rule and deciding who claims what can save your family the same.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 08 tests the math.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Which credit pays for a walk-in shower, and which pays for a separate suite?
items.detail: The Home Accessibility Tax Credit covers safety changes like a walk-in shower. The Multigenerational credit covers building a self-contained suite.

items.title: A senior on OAS and GIS owes no federal tax. What is a non-refundable credit in her name worth?
items.detail: Probably nothing. It can only lower tax she owes. A family member who pays the bill and owes tax may get more from the claim.

items.title: $8,000 of a job counts for the Home Accessibility Credit in 2026. What is the credit worth?
items.detail: $1,120, which is 14% of $8,000, to someone who owes at least that much federal tax.

items.title: What is the most the Multigenerational credit can pay for one suite?
items.detail: $7,500, which is 15% of up to $50,000 in eligible costs. It is refundable.

items.title: The contractor can start Monday, but the grant approval has not arrived. What do you do?
items.detail: Wait for written approval. Most grant programs will not pay for work that started first.

items.title: Why does the Disability Tax Credit come first in the order?
items.detail: It can take months, and it can open the accessibility credit at any age, the multigenerational credit and some provincial grants.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Three Layers

blocks.text: This week: call 211, or search your city’s name plus “home adaptation program,” and write down when applications open and the rule about starting work. Ask whether anyone in the home should apply for the Disability Tax Credit. Then have the who-pays, who-claims conversation with your family, while it is still just a conversation and nobody is upset about a bathroom.
Three layers, and you wear all three.
blocks.detail: A federal credit you claim at tax time, a provincial or city grant you apply for before work starts, and the Disability Tax Credit underneath both. Sort the invoice, decide who pays and who claims, and never let a contractor’s free Monday beat a program’s start-work rule.

items.title: HATC
items.text: Home Accessibility Tax Credit. A federal credit for permanent safety and accessibility changes to a home.

items.title: MHRTC
items.text: Multigenerational Home Renovation Tax Credit. A federal credit for building a self-contained secondary unit so a senior can live with family.

items.title: DTC
items.text: Disability Tax Credit. A certification of a severe, long-term impairment that unlocks several other programs.

items.title: Refundable credit
items.text: Paid to you even if you owe no tax. A non-refundable credit only lowers tax you already owe.

items.title: Eligible expense
items.text: A cost the credit counts. For the HATC, a permanent change that makes the home safer or easier to get around.

items.title: Forgivable loan
items.text: Money you do not have to pay back, as long as you stay in the home for a set number of years.

items.title: Service manager
items.text: The city or regional office that runs a provincial housing program and takes your application.

items.title: Self-contained unit
items.text: A living space with its own entrance, kitchen, bathroom and sleeping area. This is the test for the multigenerational credit.

items.title: Start-work rule
items.text: A program rule that the work must not begin before written approval arrives. Breaking it can cost you the funding.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: 211: dial 2-1-1 anywhere in Canada for your local list of home adaptation and repair programs.
Canada Revenue Agency: 1-800-959-8281 for questions about the accessibility credit, the multigenerational credit and the Disability Tax Credit.
Community Volunteer Income Tax Program: free tax clinics that can help file the claim if money is tight.
Your provincial housing authority or your city’s service manager, for grants and forgivable loans.

blocks.text: Federal figures here are for 2026. Credit rates, cost limits and provincial income cut-offs can change every year. Check current numbers on canada.ca and your province’s program page before you rely on them.
